newsitem.title: USA: Army rejects call for outside probe in sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Army rejects call for outside probe in sex scandal.

text.p: The Congressional Black Caucus called on Wednesday for Congress to investigate allegations by five white Army women that military investigators tried to pressure them into accusing black instructors of rape.

The National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People also called for an immmediate independent investigation of the charges, but that was rejected by Army Secretary Togo West at a Pentagon meeting with NAACP President Kweisi Mfume.
West told reporters the Army would continue investigating charges of sexual harassment of female recruits on its own for now, but that Congress had a right to examine the matter if it wanted to.
West also said he worried that the charges by the white female soldiers might "taint" a much broader Army investigation into sexual harassment and rape of female recruits.

"We certainly want to make sure that any instances of sexual harassment or rape ... are rooted out and stamped out of our military," Representative Harold Ford, a Tennessee Democrat, said at a news conference held by the Congressional Black Caucus.
"But at the same time we want to make sure that race and racism are rooted out as well," Ford added.

The 39 black members of Congress asked military committees in both the Senate and the House of Representatives to conduct independent investigations of the allegations made on Tuesday by five women Army recruits at Aberdeen Proving Ground in nearby Maryland.

The five women soldiers told a news conference on Tuesday that Army investigators tried to bully them into accusing superiors of rape. Four said they refused. One said she accused a sergeant of sexual misconduct but recanted.

The Army has charged three instructors and a captain at Aberdeen with rape and four instructors with sexual harassment on the basis of allegations by nearly 50 women in the Army, including 27 who charged they were raped.

The eighth soldier was charged earlier on Wednesday. Staff Sgt. Herman Gunter, 30, was charged with two instances of rape as well as sexual harassment, assault, adultery and obstruction of justice in cases involving three trainees.
The news conference by the five women soldiers was sponsored by the NAACP, and several NAACP officials called for an independent investigation.

Mfume said at the Pentagon after meeting with West for about an hour late on Wednesday that both believed that the statements by the five women should be investigated, but that West did not want an independent investigation.

"The NAACP believes that where crimes have been committed, where because of sexual harassment women have been taken advantage of and in instances even raped, that perpetrators of those crimes must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," Mfume said.

"We also believe, however, that where that has not been the case, that there should not be this need to cast a wide net or dragnet to round up people under false pretense with false or inacccurate accusations for the sake of showing an effort."

West said at a House hearing on Wednesday he would consider an independent investigation later but was concerned that it might interfere with court-martial proceedings at Aberdeen in the Army sex scandal.
Nearly 50 Army drill sergeants and other leaders are under investigation for sexual harassment or rape of trainees at Aberdeen and Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri.

Army officials have also said more than 7,000 calls were made to a special sexual harassment telephone hotline set up after the first Aberdeen charges were filed. They said about 1,025 of the hotline allegations were being investigated.
